finding: Four of the six candidates that record lists as ELIMINATED rest on nulls taken after the lever had already gone quiet. A null from an instrument known not to fire eliminates nothing. Same void as the promotion experiment recorded in the same file, one field away.

the_distinction.re_arm_attempt: does X revive a DEAD lever? Answerable on this bench. All four were this.
the_distinction.elimination: does X kill a LIVE lever? NOT answerable here since ~17:00, and never was.
the_distinction.why_it_matters: 'I flashed and it did not fire' says flashing did not revive it. It does not say flashing did not kill it. I labelled the first as the second.

host_tree.detail: worktree pinned at 7c0bba2, verified clean after every arm

board_uptime.detail: 90 min firing vs 40 min not, but time-of-day and everything else moved with it

consequence: The prior claim 'six eliminated, one candidate remaining' is wrong. Two are eliminated on structural grounds. Four are open. Host state a reboot would clear is not the LAST candidate - it is the only one never attempted.
who_can_settle_it: linux-x1 only. Theirs is the one lever known to fire - 25 of 44 at 2x across five arms, still firing at 23:20 - so it is the only bench where a null after an intervention carries information.
my_error: Presented a table of eliminations built from post-fade nulls, in the same record whose void_experiment field explains why post-fade nulls are worthless. I applied the standard to my own promotion experiment and to mac-bench's 0/12, and not to the six-row table directly above it.
not_claimed: that the lever is any of the four
that this bench's fade and mac-bench's are the same phenomenon - that was withdrawn and stays withdrawn
